slides.say: Customers add eighteen orders to a bakery's queue each hour. The baker completes fifteen orders every forty minutes. There are sixty orders in the queue at the start. At these constant rates, how many orders are in the queue after four hours?
So the customers add orders, and the baker takes orders away. They ask how many orders are left after four hours.
at: They ask how many orders are left

slides.say: We'll solve it in three different ways. Let's start with the math way, and some order. First the customers. They add eighteen orders an hour, for four hours. Eighteen times four is seventy-two orders.

Now the baker. Fifteen orders every forty minutes. That rate is in minutes. Like in the lesson, the units must match. So we turn the four hours into minutes. Four times sixty is two hundred forty minutes.
at: Four times sixty is two hundred forty

slides.say: Forty minutes to two hundred forty minutes is times six, because forty times six is two hundred forty.
The rate is fixed, so the work goes the same way, times six. Fifteen times six is ninety orders.
Now the queue. Sixty orders at the start, plus seventy-two new ones, is a hundred thirty-two.
The baker completed ninety. A hundred thirty-two minus ninety is forty-two.
Careful with seventy-two, choice number one. That's what we get if we read fifteen orders as fifteen an hour. Then the baker does only sixty.
at: Then the baker does only sixty
Then the baker does only sixty

slides.say: So forty-two orders are in the queue. That's choice number three.
[pause] Now the math way again, but in hours. We start again from the givens. The customers add seventy-two orders, like before. Now we turn the baker's forty minutes into hours.
From minutes to hours, we divide by sixty. Forty over sixty is two thirds of an hour.
at: Forty over sixty is two thirds

slides.say: Careful, forty minutes isn't zero point four hours. An hour has sixty minutes, not a hundred.
at: forty minutes isn't zero point four

slides.say: Two thirds of an hour to four hours is times six, because two thirds times six is four.
at: two thirds times six is four

slides.say: So the baker does fifteen times six, ninety orders again. And sixty plus seventy-two minus ninety is forty-two.
[pause] Now an insight. We start again from the givens. The customers and the baker work against each other. So let's see what happens to the queue in a short time where both numbers are whole.
Two hours is a hundred twenty minutes. That's three times forty minutes.
So in two hours, the baker completes three times fifteen, forty-five orders.
In the same two hours, the customers add two times eighteen, thirty-six orders.
Forty-five minus thirty-six is nine. So the queue gets nine orders shorter every two hours.
Four hours is two times two hours. So two times nine, eighteen orders fewer.
Sixty minus eighteen is forty-two. The same answer.
I want to use this question to show you one more tool from the same idea. When one rate works against another, only the difference counts.
A printer normally prints six hours a day. It was broken for five days. Now it prints sixteen hours a day. After how many days does it catch up?
First, how far behind is it? Five days, six hours a day. Five times six is thirty hours of printing.
Now it prints sixteen hours a day. But each day it still owes its normal six. So it gains only sixteen minus six, ten extra hours a day.
Thirty hours behind, and ten extra hours a day. Thirty divided by ten is three days.
A lot of students divide thirty by sixteen. But the normal work keeps coming every day. Only the extra part closes the gap.
So catching up is the gap divided by the extra rate. Choice number three was our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: So catching up is the gap
Choice number three was our answer
